food.text: In Scandinavia and the Baltic the climate was generally too harsh for growing grapes and olives. Beer was the commoner's drink in the north, while wine was an expensive import.
Fish were a major part of the medieval diet, and a wide variety of freshwater and saltwater kinds were eaten. Cod and herring were mainstays among the northern populations.

Before the 14th century, bread was not as common among the lower classes, especially in the north where wheat was harder to grow. Unleavened flatbread of barley, rye or oats remained more common in northern and highland regions.

Since the Middle Ages, versions of the word skyr have named cultured milk products in Scandinavia, made by adding culture to skimmed milk and letting it ferment. In Norway this skyr might be eaten with bread, watered down and drunk, cooked in porridge, or mixed with sour cream as a dip for flatbread.

art.text: Church wall paintings, called kalkmalerier in Danish, are found in some 600 churches across Denmark. This is probably the highest concentration of surviving church murals anywhere in the world. Most of them date back to the Middle Ages.

With Christianity came a new iconography in Swedish churches, especially baptismal fonts, rood crosses and devotional sculptures. According to the Swedish History Museum, no other country has such a rich and comprehensive collection of medieval liturgical art.

After the Reformation in Denmark, the medieval church murals were covered with limewash (Danish: kalk). They lay hidden for centuries and were only revealed and restored during the 19th and 20th centuries.

Sweden, along with other Scandinavian countries, has unusually rich survivals of medieval church paintings and fittings. The reason is the relatively mild nature of its Reformation, and the lack of later extensive rebuilding and redecoration of its churches.
From the 12th century, Gotland was a center for sculptors. Two of them, known by later notnames, are Majestatis and Byzantios.

Runestones were added in Scandinavia until about 1130, and they flourished between 980 and 1100. Sweden leads the way with 2,800 inscriptions, and about 85% of all identified blocks are Swedish. As an art form, the runestone is specific to Nordic culture.
Danish medieval painting is almost entirely known from church frescos. Some of these come from a 16th-century artist known as the Elmelunde Master.

Danish church murals in the Gothic style are of special interest because they were painted in a manner typical of native Danish painters. They follow the Biblia pauperum approach, setting popular Old and New Testament stories side by side in typological pairings.

The earliest art made for Swedish churches was Romanesque in style. It included fabrics and gold works as well as sculpture. Swedish art has also been strongly influenced by wider European trends, especially since about 1100.
The Viklau Madonna is one of the most well-preserved wooden sculptures from the 12th century in Europe. It was made in a workshop on Gotland, which also produced rood crosses.

Swedish runestones were originally painted and combined text with ornamentation and stylized characters. Some were quite illustrative and are called image blocks. Some of the first known image-makers in Sweden were rune carvers.

war.text: In September 1000, a large naval battle was fought in the western Baltic Sea at Svolder. King Olaf of Norway faced an alliance of the Kings of Denmark and Sweden and Olaf's own enemies in Norway. It came as Norway was unifying into a single independent state and Christianity was spreading in Scandinavia.

Magnus Erlingsson was named king of Norway in 1161 at the age of five, and was the first Norwegian king to be crowned. His father Erling Skakke held the real power as earl. Magnus was killed in the Battle of Fimreite in 1184 against the forces of Sverre Sigurdsson, who became King of Norway.

In medieval Scandinavia, arson was used in blood feuds and political conflicts to assassinate an opponent. Attackers would pile wood, brush and other combustible material against a home and set it on fire. They typically surrounded the house to prevent its inhabitants escaping, though women, the elderly and small children were sometimes allowed to leave, leaving the rest to burn.

According to the Saga of King Olaf I Tryggvason, Olaf had 60 warships plus 11 from the Jomvikings when he was ambushed by Svein Forkbeard, Olof Skötkonung and Eirik Hákonarson. The sagas say the Danes and Swedes were repulsed with heavy casualties, then Eirik cleared Olaf's ships one by one by fierce attack, the Ormen Lange last of all. Jarl Eirik took it as Olaf threw himself into the sea; Danish sources say this was suicide, preferring it to death at the enemy's hands.

Around 1010, members of Gunnar's clan burned Bergthorshvoll, the home of Njáll Þorgeirsson, killing him, his wife Bergþóra, his sons Helgi and Skarphéðinn, and his grandson Þórður. In the saga's account, the women threw whey on the fire and quenched it, until the attackers set fire to the roof from a loft, and the women inside began to weep and wail as the hall blazed. Flosi refused any atonement and would let only the women, children and house-carles out. Njáll's son-in-law Kári Sölmundarson escaped and later killed many of the burners, and the event gave Brennu-Njáls saga its name, "The Saga of the Burning of Njáll".

Although Sweden was officially Christianized by the 12th century, the Norwegian king Sigurd the Crusader undertook a crusade against Småland in the early 12th century. Småland was the south-eastern part of the Swedish kingdom, and the campaign was officially meant to convert the locals.
Nobody knows exactly where the Battle of Svolder took place. Adam of Bremen places it in Øresund, while Icelandic sources put it near an island called Svolder, which is otherwise unknown.

After Svolder, Norway was ruled by the Jarls of Lade, allied to both the Danish Crown and the Commonwealth of Uppsala, Sweden. The same clashing interests divided Norway for decades, leading to the Battle of Nesjar and the Battle of Stiklestad. The resolution came in 1035 with the accession of Magnus the Good.

The Sturlunga saga reports that in 1253, during the Age of the Sturlungs, Gissur Þorvaldsson's Icelandic enemies made an attempt on his life in the Flugumýri Arson, but it failed. The story closely resembles the burning of Njáll: an assault on a house is faltering, so the attackers turn fire against the besieged defenders. Lee M. Hollander thought this account might have inspired the Njáll narrative, though the burning of Njáll also appears in the Landnámabók and several other sources.

One of the best known episodes of Svolder involves Einarr Þambarskelfir, an archer in King Olaf's fleet who later became a cunning politician. Heimskringla describes his attempt to kill Jarl Eirik and save the day for Olaf.

literature.text: Much of what we know about Norse myths comes from Iceland, where oral traditions from the pre-Christian inhabitants were written down in manuscripts, mainly in the 13th century. These include the Prose Edda by Snorri Sturluson and the Poetic Edda, a collection of poems from earlier traditional material.

Icelandic literature is best known for the sagas, prose stories written in Old Norse starting in the 13th century. They tell of the migration of people to Iceland and the voyages of Vikings to unexplored lands. Sagas are usually realistic and deal with actual events.

Two medieval Icelandic works are together called the Edda: the Prose Edda and the Poetic Edda. Both were recorded in Iceland during the 13th century, though they contain material reaching back into the Viking Age. They are the main sources for Norse mythology.

Around the 12th century, most writing in Scandinavia shifted to the Latin alphabet after the Christianization of Scandinavia. Runes did not vanish, though. They survived in marginal use as the medieval runes, in use from AD 1100 to 1500.

Old Norse poetry is split into two types. Eddaic poetry covers mythology or ancient heroes, in simpler meters, by anonymous authors. Skaldic poetry was usually praise for living kings and nobles, in more intricate meters, by known poets called skalds.

Snorri Sturluson wrote the Prose Edda around 1220 as a manual of poetics. It was meant to help Icelandic poets and readers grasp alliterative verse and the mythology behind skaldic kennings. It has a Prologue and three books: Gylfaginning, Skáldskaparmál and Háttatal.

Around 1200, Gunnlaugr Leifsson wrote Merlínússpá, a verse translation of Geoffrey of Monmouth's Prophetiae Merlini. It is the only translation of a foreign prose text into poetry in Old Norse-Icelandic literature. It is also the earliest Arthurian text translated in medieval Scandinavia.

In Skáldskaparmál, Snorri Sturluson recounts the myth of how Odin brought the mead of poetry to Asgard. Poets even spoke of poetry as 'the drink of the raven-god', meaning Odin. This shows how important poetry was in ancient Scandinavian culture.

The Codex Regius was written in the 13th century, but nothing is known of its whereabouts until 1643, when Bishop Brynjólfur Sveinsson obtained it. He sent it as a present to King Christian IV of Denmark. It stayed in Copenhagen's Royal Library for centuries and returned to Iceland in 1971.

Poetry could carry deep emotion inside prose sagas. Egil's Saga, for example, contains a lyrical and very emotional poem about the loss of Egil's sons. In sagas, poems often paused the story to examine an experience more closely.

Bishop Brynjólfur Sveinsson attributed the Codex Regius to Sæmundr the Learned, a 12th century Icelandic priest. Modern scholars reject this attribution. Even so, the name Sæmundar Edda is still sometimes used for the Poetic Edda.

Merlínússpá is written in fornyrðislag, the verse form also used in the prophetic poems Völuspá and Völuspá hin skamma. Its Old Norse-Icelandic imagery and meter give it the semblance of an Eddic poem. One manuscript, AM 573 4to, omits it because the scribe noted that many people know that poem.

Around 1300, a Dominican monk wrote the Fornsvenska Legendariet. Confusion between Scandinavian Dacia and Pontic Dacia led it to claim that the Roman emperor Trajan conquered Baltic Denmark instead of Pontic Dacia.

Oddr Snorrason's Saga of Olaf Tryggvason (ca. 1190) built an elaborate account of Svolder from skaldic poetry, oral history, learned European examples and an uninhibited imagination. Later sagas took it up. The immense Óláfs saga Tryggvasonar en mesta (ca. 1300) combines several sources into the last, longest and least reliable account.

science.text: Scandinavian runes did not stay fixed. In the Middle Ages the Younger Futhark was expanded so that it once more had one sign for each sound of the Old Norse language. Dotted variants marked voiced or voiceless consonants, and several new runes appeared for vowel sounds.

Since the 1950s, more than 600 inscriptions in medieval runes have been found in Bergen, mostly on wooden sticks. They are known as the Bryggen inscriptions. They show that runes were in everyday use alongside the Latin alphabet for several centuries.

Some medieval runic inscriptions are actually written in the Latin language. So runes were not just a script for Old Norse. Writers could also use the old alphabet to carry the language of the church and of learning.
Spelling in medieval Scandinavian runes was far from standardised. Inscriptions show a large number of variant rune-forms. Some letters, such as s, c and z, were often used interchangeably.

politics.text: Denmark, Norway and Sweden established their own archdioceses, answering directly to the pope, in 1104, 1154 and 1164 respectively. The Christianization of Scandinavia took place between the 9th and the 12th centuries, but converting the people took longer than converting the kings.

Cnut the Great acquired England in 1016, Denmark in 1018 and Norway in 1028, ruling all three kingdoms as the North Sea Empire. At the height of his power, from 1028 to 1035, he was the most powerful ruler in western Europe after the Holy Roman Emperor.

Scandinavia's three realms each gained an archdiocese answerable directly to the pope: Denmark in 1104, Norway in 1154 and Sweden in 1164. This gave each kingdom its own church hierarchy, with archbishoprics at Nidaros and Uppsala.

King Canute IV was murdered inside St. Albans Church in 1086 after nobles and peasants alike rebelled at his enforcing of the tithe. He had also refused to use the regional assemblies to establish new laws, as was customary. His brother Prince Benedict and seventeen other housecarls were killed along with him.

Canute IV was canonized in 1188, and when his remains were moved into Odense Cathedral the entire nation humbled itself with a three-day fast. He was not the first Dane made a saint, but he was the first king, the symbol of a more or less united Denmark, to be recognized as worthy of veneration.

A brief Swedish civil war in 1066 mainly reflected divisions between practitioners of indigenous religions and advocates of Christianity. By the mid-twelfth century the Christian faction appeared to have triumphed. The once resistant center of Uppsala became the seat of the Swedish Archbishop in 1164.

In the early 12th century the Norwegian king Sigurd the Crusader launched a crusade against Småland, the south-eastern part of the Swedish kingdom. Officially it was to convert the locals, even though Sweden was already considered Christianized by the 12th century.

After Harthacnut's death in 1042, Magnus of Norway took control of Denmark. Magnus ejected Sveyn Estridsson in 1046, but in 1047 Sveyn asked England for 50 ships to fight Magnus. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says Sveyn expelled Magnus from Denmark and "entered the country by a huge carnage". The Danes then paid him a large sum of money and recognized him as king, and the same year Magnus died.

Nicholas Breakspear, later Pope Adrian IV, visited Norway from 1152 to 1154 and set out a church structure for the country. The papal bull confirming the Norwegian archdiocese at Nidaros is dated 30 November 1154.

Harthacnut, who ruled England and Denmark, died suddenly in June 1042 "as he stood at his drink" at the wedding feast of Tovi the Proud, a Danish thegn of his father's court. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle said he never did anything royal during his entire reign.

philosophy.text: The Hávamál, a poem attributed to Odin, is considered the most important source on Old Norse philosophy. It has been called the "Nicomachean Ethics of the North". It is a poem on social conduct within the Poetic Edda.

Old Norse philosophy held that happiness could only be attained through a life of virtue. The interconnected virtues of wisdom, self-control and personal independence were central to it, and wisdom mattered most of all.

The Hávamál teaches that wealth is temporary while wisdom is eternal, and it dismisses wealth as "the most fickle of friends". It also holds that wisdom can only be acquired through experience, and that traveling is an important source of that experience.

Scholars such as Guðmundur Finnbogason and Sveinbjorn Johnson have pointed out striking similarities between Old Norse philosophy and ancient Greek philosophy, especially that of Homer and Aristotle. These similarities appear to be the result of independent development rather than outside influence.

The Prose Edda by Snorri Sturluson presents Norse deities with layers of euhemerization. Gods and supernatural beings appear either as human beings who were deified in time or as beings demonized through Christian mythology.

According to Lee M. Hollander, the Poetic Edda is as important for understanding the ethical views of the Norse and other Germanic peoples as the Vedas are for understanding Indian philosophy. He also compared it to the works of Homer for understanding ancient Greek philosophy.

culture.text: In Denmark, Harald Bluetooth declared the country Christian around 965 and raised the larger of the two Jelling Stones. Historian Anders Winroth argues that Scandinavian kings willingly adopted the religion because they saw it as politically advantageous.

For several centuries in the Middle Ages, Denmark was called Dacia, a name that really belonged to a kingdom in modern Romania. The Norman historian Dudo of Saint-Quentin first applied it in the 11th century, using false etymologies to link the Danes to the Dacians and ancient Greeks and give the Norman dukes a prestigious origin legend.

Mendicant friars spread across Scandinavia in the 13th and 14th centuries. Altogether, 96 convents were founded across Denmark, Norway and Sweden, including Estonia, Finland and Karelia. The Dominicans arrived first in 1220, followed by the Franciscans in 1232 and the Carmelites in 1410.

Adam of Bremen described the temple at Uppsala in the 11th century, saying it held idols of Borr, Thor, Odin and Frey. Nearby stood a large tree and a well where sacrifices were made. Some details of his account appear inaccurate, possibly influenced by Norse mythology.

Iceland adopted Christianity in 1000 AD under pressure from Norway. Blood feuds had particularly devastated Iceland, and the threat of a religiously motivated civil war was real. The chieftain Þorgeirr Ljósvetningagoði formulated a law making Christianity the official religion, while private religious practice stayed outside the law. This limited the feuds and avoided that civil war.

The Dominicans arrived in Scandinavia in 1220 and the Franciscans in 1232, and both chose the name Dacia for their provinces. In medieval universities, the suffix de Dacia or the adjective Dacus identified students and scholars from Denmark or Scandinavia.

Archaeology at Gamla Uppsala found that the only material remains of the rituals once performed there are of animals. Their age indicates they were deposited in March, which agrees with written sources on the Dísablót.

As Norway and other lands became Christian, traditional practices were marginalized and eventually persecuted. Völvas, practitioners of the pre-Christian tradition of seid, were executed or exiled under newly Christianized governments in the eleventh and twelfth centuries.

Olof Skötkonung, the first Christian king of Sweden, made an agreement of toleration with supporters of the cult at Uppsala. Presumably he was not powerful enough to violently enforce the observance of Christianity in Uppland. Instead he established an episcopal see at Skara around 1000, near his stronghold at Husaby.

The Dominicans arrived in Scandinavia in 1220, followed by the Franciscans in 1232, and both chose Dacia as the name for their provinces. These provinces also covered Sweden, Norway and parts of the Eastern Baltic. So Dacia could mean Denmark alone, or all three Scandinavian kingdoms.

Around the year 1300, a Dominican monk wrote the Fornsvenska Legendariet, which claims the Roman emperor Trajan conquered Baltic Denmark instead of the Dacia on the Black Sea. The mix-up came from the medieval habit of calling Denmark Dacia.

The first known church reference to Dacia dates to 1192, when Cardinal Cencius, later Pope Honorius III, called Denmark by that name in the Liber Censuum, a register of papal income. After that the term became standard in papal documents for Denmark, and sometimes for all of Scandinavia.
